core: Revenue management as a discipline: selling the right room to the right guest at the right time for the right price through the right channel
Its origin in airline yield management after 1978 deregulation, and why perishable, fixed-capacity inventory with fluctuating demand makes it work
Market segmentation, rate fences, and length-of-stay controls
Overbooking: purpose, risks (walking guests), and ethical/regulatory limits
Distribution channels and the direct-versus-OTA (commission) trade-off
Naming RevPAR as the headline performance measure and handing metric math to the sibling topic

U.S. DOT oversales rule (14 CFR Part 250) as the regulated analogue of overbooking

claims.claim: Revenue management is the discipline of allocating and pricing fixed, perishable inventory to maximize total revenue, summarized in lodging as selling the right room to the right guest at the right time for the right price through the right channel.

Revenue management originated in the airline industry: after the U.S. Airline Deregulation Act took effect in 1978, carriers set their own fares, and American Airlines under Robert Crandall pioneered controlling how many seats were released at discounted advance-purchase fares versus protected for later higher-paying travelers; Crandall popularized the term 'yield management.'

Yield/revenue management works when capacity is relatively fixed, inventory is perishable, the product is sold in advance, demand fluctuates and is uncertain, the market can be segmented by willingness to pay, and the marginal cost of a sale is low relative to fixed capacity cost.
A hotel room for a given night is perishable inventory: it cannot be stored and earns nothing if unsold for that night.
Revenue managers forecast demand from history adjusted for day of week, season, and events, and continuously compare the forecast with booking pace (pickup) to adjust rates and restrictions.

Market segmentation lets a hotel charge different guests different prices; rate fences (advance purchase, nonrefundable rates, packages) are the rules that deliver a lower price to a target segment without higher-paying guests taking the same rate.

Length-of-stay controls (such as minimum length of stay or closed-to-arrival) manage which bookings are accepted on a given night to protect more valuable multi-night demand; hotels adapted length-of-stay optimization from airline practice.

Overbooking deliberately accepts more reservations than rooms, sized to expected no-shows and cancellations, to reduce the guaranteed loss from rooms that would otherwise sit empty; the risk is having to relocate ('walk') guests if too many arrive.

The airline analogue of overbooking is regulated: under U.S. DOT rules (14 CFR Part 250), when a flight is oversold a carrier must request volunteers before involuntarily denying anyone boarding, and passengers involuntarily denied boarding are generally entitled to compensation.

Distribution channel choice affects net revenue: a direct booking (hotel website or phone) keeps the full rate, while an online travel agency (OTA) booking carries a commission but brings demand the hotel might not reach on its own, making it a trade-off rather than a channel to avoid.

RevPAR (revenue per available room) is the headline lodging performance measure combining occupancy and rate into one comparable figure; its formula and pricing arithmetic belong to the pricing and occupancy topic.
Yield/revenue management has spread beyond airlines to lodging, rental cars, cruise lines, and other capacity-constrained service firms.
Lodging managers coordinate hotel operations including front office, housekeeping, and pricing/revenue decisions; the occupation had a median annual wage of $68,130 in May 2024.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Exact dates and naming of the early airline systems (e.g., American's Super Saver fares in 1977 versus the fuller yield-management/DINAMO system implemented in the mid-to-late 1980s).
positions: Super-saver discounted advance-purchase fares appeared around 1977, before deregulation was complete
The automated seat-inventory control system was developed and fully deployed over the following decade
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states only the well-established facts: deregulation took effect in 1978, Crandall's approach released limited discounted advance-purchase seats while protecting higher-fare inventory, and Crandall popularized 'yield management.' Specific proprietary system names and precise deployment years are omitted to avoid overstating contested detail.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Hospitality and Tourism — Chapter 4: Lodging Operations
sourceRecords.notes: Open hospitality textbook chapter read via WebFetch. Defines revenue management as optimizing revenue by managing room rates, inventory, and distribution channels to 'sell the right room to the right guest at the right price and at the right time'; covers dynamic pricing, demand forecasting, inventory management across segments/channels, OTAs, and the occupancy/ADR/RevPAR metrics. Supports the definition, forecasting/inventory, distribution, and RevPAR-naming claims. Facts synthesized; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Yield Management: A Tool for Capacity-Constrained Service Firms (Journal of Operations Management, 1989)
sourceRecords.provider: Sheryl E. Kimes / Cornell University eCommons (open access copy)
sourceRecords.notes: Foundational peer-reviewed article establishing the conditions for yield management: relatively fixed capacity, perishable inventory, product sold in advance, fluctuating/uncertain demand, ability to segment markets, and low marginal sales cost relative to capacity cost, plus the airline-to-lodging extension. Verified via domain search and the open-access Cornell eCommons record. Supports the definition, perishability, why-it-works, and segmentation claims. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Revenue Management — History of O.R. Excellence
sourceRecords.provider: INFORMS (Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences)
sourceRecords.notes: Professional-society history of revenue management. Supports the origin story: U.S. airline deregulation took effect in 1978, low-fare competition drove innovation, Robert Crandall of American Airlines pioneered seat-inventory control and popularized 'yield management,' the perishable fixed-capacity problem, and the spread to hotels (length-of-stay optimization) and other industries. Page returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher; content captured via search extraction and cross-checked with Kimes. Canonical URL registered; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: 14 CFR Part 250 — Oversales
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations)
sourceRecords.notes: Federal regulation governing airline oversales/overbooking. Supports the claim that when a flight is oversold, carriers must request volunteers before involuntary denied boarding (Sec. 250.2b) and must compensate passengers involuntarily denied boarding (Secs. 250.5, 250.9). eCFR redirected the fetcher to an unblock gateway; content verified via domain-restricted search of eCFR sections. Canonical URL registered.

sourceRecords.title: Bumping & Oversales — Aviation Consumer Protection
sourceRecords.notes: DOT consumer-facing explanation of overbooking/bumping: an oversold flight has more confirmed passengers than seats; airlines must ask for volunteers before denying anyone boarding involuntarily, and involuntarily bumped passengers are generally entitled to compensation. Supports the regulated-overbooking claim in plain terms. Content verified via domain-restricted search.
